explanations.explanation: Wise it is. Joab sends to Tekoa to bring back a wise woman (2 Samuel 14:2). I think he needed someone who could carry a story to a king without tripping over it. Grabbing the first person he saw wouldn't have cut it.
Young isn't the word in the verse. Joab sends for a wise woman (2 Samuel 14:2). The text never gives her age, so I won't invent one. Wise is the whole job description.

Wealthy would make her a fancy guest, but the text says wise (2 Samuel 14:2). It says nothing about her money. Joab sends to Tekoa for a wise woman. For this plan, I think her words matter more than her purse.

It's the opposite. Joab tells her, “put on clothes for mourning and do not anoint yourself with oil.” (2 Samuel 14:2) He wants her to act like a woman who has mourned for the dead a long time. I think a nice shiny face would have spoiled the costume.

Right, the oil stays in the bottle. Joab says, “put on clothes for mourning and do not anoint yourself with oil.” (2 Samuel 14:2) He wants her to act like a woman who has mourned for the dead a long time. No glow, no shine, just the part.
Joab's words. The verse says it plainly: “And Joab put the words in her mouth.” (2 Samuel 14:3) So her sad story is a script. She's basically reading cue cards to a king.
Her own words would have made this simple, but it doesn't go that way. “And Joab put the words in her mouth.” (2 Samuel 14:3) She's the voice and he's the writer. Brave speaker, borrowed notes.

Absalom isn't the one giving the words here. Joab is the one who sends for the woman and tells her what to say (2 Samuel 14:2-3). The text never says Absalom had a hand in it. Joab is named, plain and simple.
True. Her first words are “Help me, O king!” (2 Samuel 14:4) She falls facedown first, and then she cries out. Whatever else is going on, she opens like someone who needs help.
It really is a cry for help. After falling facedown in homage, she says, “Help me, O king!” (2 Samuel 14:4) Those are her first words to David. Easy to miss with so much drama going on around them.
She says the opposite. Her sons were fighting in the field “…with no one to separate them…” (2 Samuel 14:6) Nobody stepped in. One struck the other and killed him, and that's the heart of her story.

Right, no one stepped in. In her story the two sons were fighting in the field “…with no one to separate them…” (2 Samuel 14:6) Then one struck the other and killed him. I think that detail makes the story hit harder.

explanations.answer: Put him to death for his brother's life
explanations.explanation: That's it. The clan says, “Hand over the one who struck down his brother, that we may put him to death for the life of the brother whom he killed.” (2 Samuel 14:7) It's a life for a life, and the clan wants it done. The widow only has one son left.

explanations.answer: Send him away from the land for good
explanations.explanation: Sending him away isn't what the clan says. They want to put him to death for the life of the brother he killed (2 Samuel 14:7). That's a much heavier demand than leaving the land. The widow would lose her last son.

explanations.answer: Make him a servant to the whole clan
explanations.explanation: Making him a servant isn't what the clan says. They will “…put him to death for the life of the brother whom he killed.” (2 Samuel 14:7) That's heavy, and she's pleading with the king over it. It's the life of her last son on the line.

Name. She says they would “…extinguish my one remaining ember by not preserving my husband’s name or posterity on the earth.” (2 Samuel 14:7) Her husband is already dead, so her last son carries it all. I think that's why she calls him her one remaining ember.

Flocks sound sensible, but she says nothing about animals. What won't be preserved is her husband's name or posterity on the earth (2 Samuel 14:7). That's a family loss, not a money loss. The heir is the whole point.

Silver isn't in her speech. What she's afraid of losing is her husband's name and posterity on the earth (2 Samuel 14:7). That's about family, not a bank account. You can't fit a family name in a cookie jar.

She says the opposite. “…may any blame be on me and on my father’s house, and may the king and his throne be guiltless.” (2 Samuel 14:9) She puts the blame on herself and her father's house. I think she's making it easy for him to say yes.

Right, she takes the blame herself. She says, “…may any blame be on me and on my father’s house, and may the king and his throne be guiltless.” (2 Samuel 14:9) That's a big offer to make to a king. Hold on to it, because she's not done talking.

explanations.answer: Not a hair of his head will fall
explanations.explanation: Not a hair. David vows by the LORD: “not a hair of your son’s head will fall to the ground.” (2 Samuel 14:11) A vow sworn by the LORD is serious business. And it's exactly what she asked for.

explanations.answer: The avenger will be put to death
explanations.explanation: That isn't what David says. The avenger of blood is the one she wants stopped (2 Samuel 14:11). David's vow is about her son: “not a hair of your son’s head will fall to the ground.” He protects the son and says nothing about punishing anyone.

explanations.answer: The whole clan will be banished
explanations.explanation: Banishing the clan never comes up. David's vow only covers her son: “not a hair of your son’s head will fall to the ground.” (2 Samuel 14:11) It's short, it's sworn by the LORD, and it's about one son. Keep that vow in your pocket for later.

explanations.answer: Not bringing back his own banished son
explanations.explanation: That's the one. She asks, “…does he not convict himself, since he has not brought back his own banished son?” (2 Samuel 14:13) She starts with a story about a family and ends by pointing at the king's own. That's quite the turn.

explanations.answer: Ignoring the widows of his kingdom
explanations.explanation: She says she's a widow, so I see why that sounds right. But the charge is different: “…does he not convict himself, since he has not brought back his own banished son?” (2 Samuel 14:13) Her widow story was the setup. The banished son is who she's aiming at.

explanations.answer: Breaking an old vow to the LORD
explanations.explanation: David did just make a vow (2 Samuel 14:11), but she never says he broke one. She says he “…has not brought back his own banished son?” (2 Samuel 14:13) Her story was about one family, and now she points at his. That's the turn.

True. She says, “Yet God does not take away a life, but He devises ways that the banished one may not be cast out from Him.” (2 Samuel 14:14) She says it right after bringing up David's banished son (2 Samuel 14:13). I think she wants the king to hear it for himself.

It's in there. She says, “Yet God does not take away a life, but He devises ways that the banished one may not be cast out from Him.” (2 Samuel 14:14) Those are her own words to the king. They come right after she mentions David's banished son (2 Samuel 14:13).

Inheritance. She says a man would “…cut off both me and my son from God’s inheritance.” (2 Samuel 14:16) It echoes the clan's plan to cut off the heir (2 Samuel 14:7). I think it's about more than land. It's about having a place among God's people.

No temple in her words. The man would cut her and her son off from “God’s inheritance.” (2 Samuel 14:16) I think that's about belonging, not about a building. Her fear is about her son and her family line.

No altar in this speech. She says the man would “…cut off both me and my son from God’s inheritance.” (2 Samuel 14:16) Her fear stays on her son and her husband's line. Same worry as before, just said another way.

She does the opposite. David asks, “Is the hand of Joab behind all this?” and she answers, “…Joab is the one who gave me orders; he told your maidservant exactly what to say.” (2 Samuel 14:19) She owns up. After all that acting, the truth comes out quick.

Right, she owns up. David asks, “Is the hand of Joab behind all this?” (2 Samuel 14:19) And she says, “…Joab is the one who gave me orders; he told your maidservant exactly what to say.” No dodging. The truth comes out.
That's it. David tells Joab, “I hereby grant this request. Go, bring back the young man Absalom.” (2 Samuel 14:21) Joab wrote the script, and now he's the one getting the order. The plan worked.

explanations.answer: Go and send the woman home
explanations.explanation: David already told her to go home back in verse 8. Now he turns to Joab with a new order: “Go, bring back the young man Absalom.” (2 Samuel 14:21) The woman's part is done. This order is about Absalom.

explanations.answer: Go and punish Absalom in Geshur
explanations.explanation: Punishing him isn't what David says. He tells Joab, “Go, bring back the young man Absalom.” (2 Samuel 14:21) Bring him back, not hunt him down. And Joab does go and bring him (2 Samuel 14:23).
Jerusalem. Joab got up, went to Geshur, and brought Absalom to Jerusalem (2 Samuel 14:23). Verse 28 says Absalom lived in Jerusalem two years (2 Samuel 14:28). So that's where the trip ends.
Hebron isn't the stop here. Joab goes to Geshur and brings Absalom to Jerusalem (2 Samuel 14:23). Verse 28 says Absalom lived in Jerusalem two years. So it's Jerusalem all the way.

Bethlehem isn't named here. Joab goes to Geshur and brings Absalom to Jerusalem (2 Samuel 14:23). Absalom is later said to be living in Jerusalem (2 Samuel 14:28). The text gives Jerusalem as the destination.

explanations.answer: He must not see the king's face
explanations.explanation: That's the condition. David says, “He may return to his house, but he must not see my face.” (2 Samuel 14:24) So Absalom is home, but he doesn't see his father. Close by, and still shut out.

explanations.answer: He must stay outside the city walls
explanations.explanation: Nothing about walls. Absalom may return to his house (2 Samuel 14:24), and verse 28 has him living in Jerusalem. The condition is about the king's face. David says, “…he must not see my face.”

explanations.answer: He must never speak to Joab again
explanations.explanation: Joab isn't in the condition at all. David's words are, “…he must not see my face.” (2 Samuel 14:24) Absalom even sends for Joab later (2 Samuel 14:29). The rule is about the king, not about Joab.
Joab “…refused to come to him.” (2 Samuel 14:29) Absalom sent for him, and Joab just wouldn't show. Joab is the one who helped bring Absalom back, so you'd expect a visit. Not this time.
Joab doesn't come right away. The verse says he “…refused to come to him.” (2 Samuel 14:29) Absalom sends for him and gets no visit. Keep that in mind, because it matters in the next verses.
No servant in this verse. Joab “…refused to come to him.” (2 Samuel 14:29) The text gives no stand-in, only a no. A plain no is hard to miss.
It's the other way around. Absalom sends a second time, but “…Joab still would not come.” (2 Samuel 14:29) Two tries, two no's. Joab doesn't show up either time.
Right, still no. Absalom sends a second time, and “…Joab still would not come.” (2 Samuel 14:29) That's two messages and nobody at the door. I think a person could get pretty annoyed by that.
Fire. Absalom tells his servants, “Go and set it on fire!” (2 Samuel 14:30) And they do. That's not a subtle way of saying, “please answer my message.”
Harvesting is a quiet plan, and Absalom's isn't quiet. He says, “Go and set it on fire!” (2 Samuel 14:30) And the servants set the field on fire. Fire is the plan, not harvesting.

Trampling would be messy, but the text says fire: “Go and set it on fire!” (2 Samuel 14:30) Absalom's servants set Joab's field on fire. That's a loud way to get someone's attention. And it worked, as the next verse shows.

Geshur. Absalom says, “Why have I come back from Geshur? It would be better for me if I were still there.” (2 Samuel 14:32) I think he means being home without seeing the king feels worse than being away. That's a sad thing to say.

Egypt isn't in this chapter. Absalom asks, “Why have I come back from Geshur?” (2 Samuel 14:32) Geshur is the place Joab went to bring him from (2 Samuel 14:23). So that's where he says he'd rather be.

Tekoa is where the wise woman comes from (2 Samuel 14:2), not where Absalom was. He asks, “Why have I come back from Geshur?” (2 Samuel 14:32) Geshur is the place Joab went to bring him from (2 Samuel 14:23). Two different places, easy to mix up.

True. Absalom says, “So now, let me see the king’s face, and if there is iniquity in me, let him kill me.” (2 Samuel 14:32) He asks to see the king's face, and he adds that if there is iniquity in him, the king should kill him. That's a bold thing to say.

It's in there. Absalom says, “So now, let me see the king’s face, and if there is iniquity in me, let him kill me.” (2 Samuel 14:32) He asks to see the king's face, and he also says that if there is iniquity in him, the king should kill him. I think he wants the waiting to end.
He kisses Absalom. After Absalom bows facedown, “Then the king kissed Absalom.” (2 Samuel 14:33) After two years of not seeing the king's face, that's a big moment. I think it means a lot.

explanations.answer: He sends him back to Geshur
explanations.explanation: No sending back. David summons Absalom, he bows facedown, and “Then the king kissed Absalom.” (2 Samuel 14:33) Geshur is where Absalom was before Joab brought him home (2 Samuel 14:23). This scene goes a different way.

explanations.answer: He orders him out of the city
explanations.explanation: No orders to leave. David summons Absalom, and when he bows facedown, “Then the king kissed Absalom.” (2 Samuel 14:33) After the long wait, the king greets him. Nothing in the verse sends him away.
